title: Bubble charts: scale the third measure by area
summary: Use two positions and one area measure without letting radius scaling, overlap or missing records distort the comparison.
body:
Use two positions and one area measure without letting radius scaling, overlap or missing records distort the comparison.

Three measures require three separate contracts

A bubble chart is a scatterplot whose marker area carries another nonnegative quantity. Position answers two questions; size answers a third. In an operations review, horizontal position could be median minutes to close a ticket, vertical position the fraction that breached a service target, and circle area the number of open tickets. Those measures come from different aggregations, so write the population and period beside each one. A depot with no measured closure time does not belong at zero minutes. Keep it in an excluded-record table instead of placing it at the origin. Likewise, a zero open-ticket count can be represented as a zero-area mark in the source table, but it cannot be selected on a chart. Show the count in an adjacent row or give zero-count depots a clearly labeled outline symbol with a fixed visual size that is not part of the area scale. Encoding choice and grain should be settled before selecting colors.

Area, not diameter, carries volume

A circle's area grows with the square of its diameter. Setting diameter directly proportional to a count makes 81 tickets look nine times wider and 81 times larger than nine tickets, despite a true ninefold count difference. To make area proportional to count, set diameter to a fixed maximum diameter times the square root of count divided by the maximum count. In the worked ledger, depots with nine, 36 and 81 open tickets receive diameters of 12, 24 and 36 pixels when the largest bubble is 36 pixels wide. Their areas then have the same 1:4:9 ratio as their counts. A plotting library may accept area in points squared instead of diameter in pixels; inspect that API rather than applying the square root twice. Display at least two labeled reference circles and the actual numeric value on focus or in a table. Proportional map symbols face the same area problem.

Overlap can erase the observation that matters

Large bubbles drawn last can hide smaller ones at nearly identical coordinates. Sort by descending size before drawing so smaller circles remain on top, add a visible stroke, and use moderate transparency only if overlapping colors have a meaningful legend. Transparency alone does not reveal every record when several points coincide. Offer a list of the observations at the selected coordinate, and preserve stable depot IDs in that list. Do not jitter either quantitative axis unless the adjustment is disclosed and the original values are still available. For dense data, switch to a hexbin or density view for the first scan, then open the original bubbles through a filter. A third encoded variable adds visual load; a fourth color measure should be used only when it answers an explicit question. Overplotting and hexbins explain the fallback.

Freeze the comparison frame

When two periods are placed side by side, keep the horizontal range, vertical range and maximum-bubble reference the same. Rescaling each panel independently can make a decline in ticket volume look like no change at all. The chart must state whether the size measure is a count, rate or monetary total; negative quantities cannot use an ordinary area scale without a separate sign channel. If a filter removes the largest depot, retain the original size reference when the user is comparing filtered and unfiltered views. Supply an accessible table with depot, both positional measures, ticket count and exclusion reason. If the story is primarily about count rank, bars will usually be faster to read than circles. Shared-scale panels, keyboard access and export contracts cover the handoff.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite, sqrt

def prepare_depot_bubbles(depot_rows, maximum_diameter=36):
    if (not depot_rows or isinstance(maximum_diameter, bool) or
            not isinstance(maximum_diameter, (int, float)) or
            not isfinite(maximum_diameter) or maximum_diameter <= 0):
        raise ValueError("rows and a positive maximum diameter are required")
    known = set()
    for depot, close_minutes, breach_fraction, open_tickets in depot_rows:
        if not depot or depot in known:
            raise ValueError("depot IDs must be unique")
        known.add(depot)
        if (any(isinstance(value, bool) or not isinstance(value, (int, float))
                or not isfinite(value) for value in (close_minutes, breach_fraction)) or
                close_minutes < 0 or not 0 <= breach_fraction <= 1 or
                isinstance(open_tickets, bool) or not isinstance(open_tickets, int) or
                open_tickets < 0):
            raise ValueError("invalid depot measures")
    maximum_count = max(row[3] for row in depot_rows)
    if maximum_count == 0:
        raise ValueError("all zero counts need a different chart")
    marks = []
    for depot, close_minutes, breach_fraction, open_tickets in depot_rows:
        diameter = maximum_diameter * sqrt(open_tickets / maximum_count)
        marks.append((depot, close_minutes, breach_fraction,
                      open_tickets, round(diameter, 2)))
    return sorted(marks, key=lambda mark: (-mark[3], mark[0]))

depots = [("Harbor", 31, 0.12, 9),
          ("Ridge", 47, 0.19, 36),
          ("Canal", 54, 0.27, 81)]
marks = prepare_depot_bubbles(depots)
assert [(mark[0], mark[4]) for mark in marks] == [
    ("Canal", 36.0), ("Ridge", 24.0), ("Harbor", 12.0)]
assert 81 / 9 == (36 / 12) ** 2

Performance and operating cost

For N depots, validation, maximum-count lookup and diameter calculation take O(N) time. Sorting by count for a deliberate draw order takes O(N log N) time and O(N) output space. This preparation does not solve geometric overlap; a naive pairwise collision test takes O(N²), so large interactive charts should use spatial indexing or aggregate to a density view. The size reference is computed once from the full comparison set, then held fixed across related panels and filters. Rendering libraries differ on whether their size parameter means area, radius or diameter, so test the displayed reference circles against the numeric contract.

Common Mistakes

  • Setting circle diameter directly proportional to count and exaggerating area differences.
  • Changing the largest-circle reference separately for each comparison panel.
  • Using missing x or y measurements as zero and placing records at the origin.
  • Hiding coincident points behind a large opaque marker with no accessible record list.
  • Adding color as a fourth measure without a question, legend or readable alternative.

Validation drill

Prepare a depot review with 47 locations. Choose one period and one grain, hold the area reference fixed across two panels, then verify that a depot with four times another depot's count has twice its diameter rather than four times its diameter.

title: Marimekko charts: make width, height and area reconcile
summary: Build variable-width stacked columns from a counted ledger and explain the distinct denominators behind column width, segment height and cell area.
body:
Build variable-width stacked columns from a counted ledger and explain the distinct denominators behind column width, segment height and cell area.

Start with one counted cross-tab

A Marimekko chart divides a rectangle into columns of unequal width, then stacks categories within each column. One counted ledger must drive every dimension: the column total determines width, a cell divided by its column total determines height, and the same cell divided by the grand total determines rectangle area. These are three related but different questions. For support channels by outcome, a wide channel is common in the entire population; a tall Escalated segment means a high escalation share within that channel. Neither alone proves which channel contributes the most escalations overall. Count records once, define the period and clarify whether the cell count is tickets, interactions or customers. A customer who opened three tickets contributes three tickets if tickets are the declared grain. Grain and denominator and mosaic plots cover the adjoining accounting ideas.

Derive geometry from counts

The sample ledger totals 116 tickets across Web, Phone and Partner channels. Web holds 38, Phone 50 and Partner 28, so their horizontal shares are 38/116, 50/116 and 28/116. Within Phone, 25 of 50 tickets are Escalated; that cell is half the Phone column's height but only 25/116 of the whole chart area. The code returns both conditional and joint shares for every cell, then checks that all cell areas sum to one. Keep the channel order fixed between periods. A category missing from one channel gets a zero-height cell in the data table, not a fabricated sliver. Categories with no counts anywhere can leave the comparison, but state the universe used for the display. Stacked bars are easier when the column volumes are similar or only within-channel rates matter.

Area is hard to read precisely

A narrow column can contain a tall segment that still has little area. If the viewer needs to compare exact escalation rates, label the percentages or pair the chart with a sorted bar chart. If the viewer needs exact contribution to all escalations, show counts or joint shares beside the chart. Do not place a single legend percentage against every segment because each conditional percentage has a different column denominator. Avoid text inside cells too small to hold it: give those records an external label, a keyboard-accessible table and a search path. Color should identify outcomes consistently across columns, and cell borders should remain visible without relying solely on color. Text alternatives and diverging stacks offer related approaches.

Use the right comparison for change

Two Marimekko panels can be compared only if their column and category definitions are the same and both panels disclose their population sizes. If the population grows, the second panel still fills the same rectangle; its areas communicate shares, not absolute growth. Show the grand totals in the titles, or pair the panels with a count chart. Keep the same outcome colors and category ordering, and do not reorder columns by a changed rank if the task is to track a channel over time. Very small columns may vanish on a mobile viewport. Collapse the display to a table or offer a focused single-channel view rather than making touch targets thinner than a finger. The export should include the original counts, column totals, conditional shares and joint shares, not just the rendered coordinates. Export manifests and small multiples make repeat views auditable.

Worked contract

from collections import Counter

def prepare_channel_mekko(ticket_counts, channel_order, outcome_order):
    if not ticket_counts or not channel_order or not outcome_order:
        raise ValueError("counts and category orders are required")
    if (len(set(channel_order)) != len(channel_order) or
            len(set(outcome_order)) != len(outcome_order)):
        raise ValueError("category order contains duplicates")
    known_channels, known_outcomes = set(channel_order), set(outcome_order)
    cells = Counter()
    for channel, outcome, count in ticket_counts:
        if (channel not in known_channels or outcome not in known_outcomes or
                isinstance(count, bool) or not isinstance(count, int) or count < 0):
            raise ValueError("invalid counted cell")
        cells[(channel, outcome)] += count
    totals = {channel: sum(cells[(channel, outcome)] for outcome in outcome_order)
              for channel in channel_order}
    if any(total == 0 for total in totals.values()):
        raise ValueError("each displayed column needs a positive total")
    grand_total = sum(totals.values())
    columns, left = [], 0.0
    for channel in channel_order:
        width = totals[channel] / grand_total
        bottom, segments = 0.0, []
        for outcome in outcome_order:
            count = cells[(channel, outcome)]
            height = count / totals[channel]
            segments.append({"outcome": outcome, "count": count,
                             "height": height, "area": count / grand_total,
                             "bottom": bottom})
            bottom += height
        assert abs(bottom - 1) < 1e-12
        columns.append({"channel": channel, "left": left,
                        "width": width, "total": totals[channel],
                        "segments": segments})
        left += width
    assert abs(left - 1) < 1e-12
    return grand_total, columns

ticket_counts = [
    ("Web", "Closed", 21), ("Web", "Escalated", 8), ("Web", "Open", 9),
    ("Phone", "Closed", 17), ("Phone", "Escalated", 25), ("Phone", "Open", 8),
    ("Partner", "Closed", 12), ("Partner", "Escalated", 6),
    ("Partner", "Open", 10),
]
grand_total, columns = prepare_channel_mekko(
    ticket_counts, ["Web", "Phone", "Partner"],
    ["Closed", "Escalated", "Open"])
assert grand_total == 116
assert [column["total"] for column in columns] == [38, 50, 28]
assert columns[1]["segments"][1]["height"] == 0.5
assert columns[1]["segments"][1]["area"] == 25 / 116
assert abs(sum(segment["area"] for column in columns
               for segment in column["segments"]) - 1) < 1e-12

Performance and operating cost

With R counted rows, C displayed columns and O outcomes, aggregation takes O(R) expected time and O(CO) cell storage. Constructing the full rectangular grid takes O(CO) time and space even when some observed cells are absent; those cells retain explicit zero counts. A fixed category order lets a renderer place rectangles in one pass. Floating-point coordinates may not sum to exactly one, so the tests use a small tolerance while the underlying integer counts remain authoritative. Do not round each cell percentage before computing positions: independent rounding creates gaps, overlaps and totals that no longer reconcile.

Common Mistakes

  • Giving every column equal width while claiming to show its share of the total.
  • Reading conditional segment height as the segment's contribution to all records.
  • Rounding percentages before laying out the rectangles and losing reconciliation.
  • Comparing equal-sized panels as absolute totals without stating their different population sizes.
  • Putting text only inside narrow cells that cannot be read or focused.

Validation drill

Build a channel-by-outcome ledger for 47 reporting units. Reconcile row, column and grand totals; label one cell with both its within-channel share and its joint share; then test the chart at a mobile width without discarding the small cells.

  • Stacked bars: separate composition from volume and preserve denominators
  • Aggregation grain and denominator: make every plotted mark auditable

title: Circle packing: compare leaves without misreading parent circles
summary: Prepare a hierarchy for nested circles, count only leaves, and distinguish proportional leaf area from the whitespace inside enclosing parents.
body:
Prepare a hierarchy for nested circles, count only leaves, and distinguish proportional leaf area from the whitespace inside enclosing parents.

Containment communicates ancestry first

Circle packing nests child circles inside larger enclosing circles. The visible enclosure answers where a leaf belongs, while a leaf's area can encode a count. These meanings are easy to mix. A parent circle encloses child circles plus empty space, so its visible area is generally not a precise representation of the sum of its children's counts. Do not place a parent total on the same area scale as leaves and invite literal area comparison. Show exact totals in labels or a companion table. Use a full-path identifier for every node: Open under Dispatch and Open under Billing are different leaves. In a service queue ledger, count each ticket in exactly one terminal queue. If the same ticket can belong to multiple queues, change the measure to queue assignments or choose another view. Treemaps use space more efficiently, while sunbursts show ancestry in rings.

Calculate weights before drawing circles

Build totals upward from terminal leaves, never by adding a separately entered parent value to its children. A leaf with count 16 needs four times the area of a leaf with count four, which means twice the radius before any layout scaling. The worked code computes both prefix totals and target leaf radii, and verifies the root total. A packing algorithm then moves the circles to fit within their enclosing parents, often scaling them together. Padding and the arrangement of siblings introduce empty space. A stable label order and stable layout seed matter in recurring reports, or viewers will mistake a rearranged cluster for a changed relationship. Preserve leaf identifiers through layout updates. Grain and export manifests keep the geometric view tied to its ledger.

Small leaves need another route to inspection

If a leaf's rendered diameter is smaller than a usable touch or focus target, do not rely on the circle for discovery. Provide a searchable hierarchy table with full path, leaf count and parent share; let users focus a row and highlight the circle. Labels should not be forcibly clipped into tiny circles. Put full paths in the table and display only short names where there is enough room. A branch with hundreds of tiny leaves may need a drill-down action with an explicit breadcrumb back to the parent. Grouping them as Other is valid only within one parent and with a declared threshold; the original leaves must remain in the data export. Keyboard focus and text alternatives are part of the chart, not optional extras.

Choose the view for the comparison

A packed-circle diagram is good for exploring a hierarchy and spotting dominant leaves within a branch. It is weak for precise ranking of leaves scattered across different parents because people compare circle areas poorly and blank packing space interferes with apparent size. For rank questions, pair the diagram with a bar chart sorted by count. For proportional share across the entire hierarchy, a treemap may waste less space. For following a path from root to leaf, a sunburst can make depth more explicit. Keep the same top-level colors and comparable scale across updates, and state whether the geometry was recalculated after a filter. A filter that removes a branch should not silently make every surviving leaf look larger when the task is to compare before and after. Scale integrity and linked filters apply even without visible axes.

Worked contract

from collections import Counter
from math import isclose, pi, sqrt

def prepare_queue_pack(leaf_counts):
    if not leaf_counts:
        raise ValueError("leaf counts are required")
    totals, seen = Counter(), set()
    for path, count in leaf_counts:
        if (not isinstance(path, tuple) or len(path) != 3 or
                any(not isinstance(label, str) or not label.strip()
                    for label in path) or path in seen or
                isinstance(count, bool) or not isinstance(count, int) or count <= 0):
            raise ValueError("each unique leaf needs three labels and a positive count")
        seen.add(path)
        for depth in range(4):
            totals[path[:depth]] += count
    leaves = {path: sqrt(count / pi) for path, count in leaf_counts}
    assert totals[()] == sum(leaf_counts[index][1]
                             for index in range(len(leaf_counts)))
    return totals, leaves

queue_leaves = [
    (("Operations", "Dispatch", "Open"), 16),
    (("Operations", "Dispatch", "Closed"), 4),
    (("Operations", "Returns", "Open"), 9),
    (("Operations", "Returns", "Closed"), 7),
    (("Finance", "Billing", "Open"), 13),
    (("Finance", "Billing", "Closed"), 11),
]
totals, radii = prepare_queue_pack(queue_leaves)
assert totals[()] == 60
assert totals[("Operations",)] == 36
assert isclose(radii[("Operations", "Dispatch", "Open")] /
               radii[("Operations", "Dispatch", "Closed")], 2)
assert isclose(pi * radii[("Finance", "Billing", "Open")] ** 2, 13)

Performance and operating cost

For R leaf rows and fixed depth D, deriving prefix totals takes O(RD) time and O(N) space for N distinct nodes. Computing one target radius per leaf takes O(R) time and space. These are weights, not final coordinates. The packing step depends on the renderer and its padding/layout algorithm; it may alter absolute radii while preserving relative leaf areas. Do not use enclosing-parent pixel area as an exact sum because it includes blank regions. For a large tree, prepare a compact table and allow branch-by-branch exploration rather than drawing all leaves as subpixel circles.

Common Mistakes

  • Counting a parent value again after already summing its leaves.
  • Comparing enclosing parent-circle area as though empty packing space were data.
  • Using equal radius instead of equal area for equal leaf counts.
  • Merging leaves with the same short label under different parents.
  • Making tiny circles the only path to discover or select small categories.

Validation drill

Prepare a three-level queue tree with 47 terminal categories. Reconcile each branch from leaves, compute target leaf areas, and create a companion table that allows a reader to find every small leaf even when its rendered circle cannot hold a label.

  • Sunburst charts: reconcile the leaf ledger before drawing rings
  • Aggregation grain and denominator: make every plotted mark auditable
  • Interactive charts: make selection work without a pointer

summary: Choose charts from the question, unit, denominator, and uncertainty the reader needs to judge.
body:
Choose charts from the question, unit, denominator, and uncertainty the reader needs to judge.

Where to begin

Start with the decision a reader must make. Then choose an encoding that preserves the relevant comparison, define the aggregation grain, and check scale, distribution, small samples, accessibility, and dashboard provenance. The linked project turns those choices into a reviewable operations display.

Read the track

  • Aggregation grain and denominator: make every plotted mark auditable
  • Axis scales, baselines and labels: prevent a correct number from telling a false story
  • Distribution plots: keep the tail, missing values and bin policy visible
  • Uncertainty on charts: show denominators and intervals beside estimates
  • Accessible charts: encode meaning without relying on color alone

  • Data Visualization: Projects

Choose the right method

A chart with many filters can become expensive to compute and hard to interpret. Pre-aggregate only at a grain that preserves the intended question, and state when a denominator or sample size changes under a filter.

Common Mistakes

Do not truncate an axis without making the effect visible. Color alone must not carry status, and a tidy dashboard does not prove that its source query is correct.

title: Dense scatterplots: reveal overlap without hiding rare observations
summary: Use density cells and deliberate sampling when points overlap, while retaining the populations and exceptions that matter.
body:
Use density cells and deliberate sampling when points overlap, while retaining the populations and exceptions that matter.

Overplotting changes what a point means

A scatterplot maps paired values to two position channels. When thousands of records land on the same pixels, the visible mark count no longer approximates the record count. Transparency can expose a dense center, but repeated strokes saturate and rare points can disappear beneath it. Before changing the mark style, count records per screen-space cell and inspect whether the question is about density, outliers, groups or exact cases. The chart question determines whether a point cloud is still the right view.

Bin at a declared resolution

A two-dimensional density grid counts observations inside fixed x and y intervals. It can show population structure without rendering every dot. The cells need axis units, bounds and bin width; changing cell size changes the picture. A cell count is not a probability unless divided by the declared population or area. Use the same grid for comparisons across cohorts, otherwise apparent hot spots may be a change in binning. Preserve a drill-down path to the original records where access rules permit it. A heatmap of density has the same color-domain obligations as any other heatmap.

Sampling is a data product

Uniform sampling can make a common cluster readable yet omit a rare but important failure mode. If the operational question concerns unusual refunds, retain those cases deliberately and label the sample design. A stratified sample can hold a fixed number from each category, but its plotted mix no longer reflects population proportions unless weights or counts are shown. Never present sampled points as the full dataset. Record the random seed, inclusion rule and population size. The sampling frame matters even when the result is only exploratory.

Separate trend from uncertainty

A diagonal cloud does not by itself establish a causal effect. Outliers, groups and repeated measures can alter the apparent slope. Show marginal distributions or group facets when one cluster masks another. If a fitted trend is added, distinguish raw marks from the fitted line and state whether the fit is weighted, filtered or calculated on the visible sample. Influence checks are needed before treating that line as a stable summary. A truncated axis can also make a weak relation seem strong.

Validate at the pixel budget

Test identical coordinates, boundary points, non-finite values and a small rare cohort. Count how many records end in each visible density cell, then reconcile the total with the filtered input. Hovering a cell should report its count and ranges, not invent a single representative record. At high density, compare a grid and a sampled-point layer side by side: the grid describes mass, while the points retain individual exceptions. On a small screen, favor one readable layer over simultaneous translucent layers that obscure both.

Worked contract

from math import floor, isfinite

def density_cells(points: list[tuple[float, float]],
                  x_bounds: tuple[float, float],
                  y_bounds: tuple[float, float],
                  columns: int, rows: int) -> dict[tuple[int, int], int]:
    x_low, x_high = x_bounds
    y_low, y_high = y_bounds
    if columns < 1 or rows < 1 or x_low >= x_high or y_low >= y_high:
        raise ValueError("invalid grid")
    counts: dict[tuple[int, int], int] = {}
    for amount, handling_minutes in points:
        if not all(map(isfinite, (amount, handling_minutes))):
            raise ValueError("non-finite observation")
        if not (x_low <= amount <= x_high and
                y_low <= handling_minutes <= y_high):
            raise ValueError("point outside declared domain")
        column = min(columns - 1, floor((amount - x_low) * columns / (x_high - x_low)))
        row = min(rows - 1, floor((handling_minutes - y_low) * rows / (y_high - y_low)))
        counts[(column, row)] = counts.get((column, row), 0) + 1
    return counts

cells = density_cells([(47, 18), (47, 18), (81, 39)],
                      (0, 100), (0, 50), 5, 5)
assert sum(cells.values()) == 3 and max(cells.values()) == 2

Performance and operating cost

For N points and C occupied cells, fixed-grid counting takes O(N) time and O(C) memory, with C no larger than the number of grid positions. Rendering one rectangle per occupied cell can be much cheaper than rendering N circles. The example rejects out-of-domain points; a production view may instead maintain an explicit overflow bucket, but it must label that choice. Recompute bins when the axis domain or pixel resolution changes, and do not confuse screen-density counts with a probability density estimate.

Common Mistakes

  • Lowering opacity and assuming the visible marks still represent all records.
  • Sampling rare cases away while evaluating an exception-handling workflow.
  • Comparing density grids built with different bounds or cell widths.
  • Calling a fitted slope causal based on a crowded scatterplot.

Validation drill

Generate 4,700 routine handling cases plus 31 rare high-delay cases. Compare raw points, a fixed grid and a seeded stratified sample; report whether each view keeps the rare cluster visible and whether displayed counts reconcile.

title: Proportional-symbol maps: size circles by area, not radius
summary: Declare the location meaning and value unit, then preserve zero, overlap and boundary context.
body:
Declare the location meaning and value unit, then preserve zero, overlap and boundary context.

A symbol has a location contract

A circle over a map may represent a precise facility, a regional centroid or an approximate address. Those are not equivalent. State what the coordinate means and how much location precision the data support. Choropleth maps color whole regions; proportional symbols encode a value at a point or chosen anchor. Do not place a regional total at a centroid without telling the reader that the circle summarizes an area. If location is sensitive, aggregate or coarsen before publication rather than relying on small marker size to conceal it.

Area should represent quantity

If a symbol encodes a nonnegative count, its visual area should be proportional to that count. Doubling the radius multiplies area by four, exaggerating the larger value. Compute radius from the square root of value relative to a declared maximum. Use a visible reference legend with at least two example magnitudes. A zero count should remain a recorded zero, even if its circle has no area; a tiny outline or table entry may be needed to keep the location discoverable. Scale integrity also means fixing the size domain across maps intended for comparison.

Overlapping circles need an explicit policy

Dense areas can hide smaller symbols under larger ones. Drawing order, opacity and zoom can all change what a reader sees. Try smaller maximum radius, outlines, clustering with disclosed counts, or an alternate ranked table. Do not let overlap remove records from the export. Hexbin density may be better when the question is where point events concentrate, while a proportional-symbol map is better when each point already has a meaningful aggregate. Test overlapping facilities at the closest supported zoom and on a narrow phone viewport.

Count and rate are different maps

A large population center may dominate a count map while having a modest per-person rate. A rate can be mapped with symbol size only if the legend names its denominator and the sampling uncertainty is not buried. Often a count-sized symbol plus a separately encoded rate is too much for one map; use paired maps or a table. The denominator contract must follow the geography and period. Export ID, coordinate meaning, count, denominator, computed rate, symbol radius and suppression state, so the map can be checked without its pixels.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite, sqrt

def area_scaled_radii(values: dict[str, float],
                      maximum_radius: float) -> dict[str, float]:
    if not isfinite(maximum_radius) or maximum_radius <= 0:
        raise ValueError("maximum radius must be positive")
    if not values or any(not place for place in values):
        raise ValueError("locations must be named")
    if any(not isfinite(value) or value < 0 for value in values.values()):
        raise ValueError("mapped values must be finite and nonnegative")
    maximum_value = max(values.values())
    if maximum_value == 0:
        return {place: 0.0 for place in values}
    return {place: maximum_radius * sqrt(value / maximum_value)
            for place, value in values.items()}

service_calls = {"north depot": 47, "south depot": 188, "west depot": 0}
radii = area_scaled_radii(service_calls, 20)
assert radii["south depot"] == 20
assert radii["north depot"] == 10
assert radii["west depot"] == 0

Performance and operating cost

For N locations, finding the maximum and calculating radii takes O(N) time and O(N) output space. The code sizes nonnegative values by area and leaves geographic projection, collision handling and legend generation to the map renderer. A production map must keep one fixed reference maximum across views that readers are expected to compare; recalculating it after every filter changes apparent size.

Common Mistakes

  • Making radius proportional to count and thereby exaggerating area.
  • Treating a regional centroid as an exact event location.
  • Letting large symbols cover small ones without a table or overlap strategy.
  • Comparing maps whose size domains were auto-scaled independently.

Validation drill

Map 59 service depots with zero, small and large call counts. Use area-scaled circles, disclose the location meaning and produce a fixed-size legend for two reporting periods.

title: Hexbin density: count overlapping points without hiding exposure
summary: Declare coordinates, bin resolution and whether color means count or rate.
body:
Declare coordinates, bin resolution and whether color means count or rate.

Overplotting is a counting problem

When thousands of marks overlap, a dark patch can reflect drawing order or opacity rather than a trustworthy count. Binning makes the count explicit. A hexagonal grid offers a compact neighborhood shape, but it still imposes a resolution and origin. Record both. Overplotting and sampling bias explain why a random sample may help inspection but cannot silently replace total-density reporting. Show how many points survived filtering and coordinate validation before any bins are painted.

Coordinate units determine the grid

A grid in longitude and latitude degrees does not represent equal ground area across latitudes. For a geographic density question, project coordinates into an appropriate metric system before choosing cell width. If this is only a relative screen-space view, say so and avoid claims about area-normalized risk. Keep projection, extent and grid origin fixed across time panels. Otherwise unchanged points may fall into different cells. Geographic rate maps have a related denominator problem.

Count and exposure answer different questions

A cell with 81 incidents may cover 810,000 journeys; a cell with 47 may cover 4,700. Count highlights workload, while incidents per journey describe a different quantity. Preserve zero-exposure cells separately from zero-incident cells. Dividing by drawn polygon area does not produce a population risk. The denominator contract must match the decision. If sparse cells are suppressed for privacy, label that suppression and retain a public aggregate total rather than pretending the hidden cells are zero.

Test resolution and edge effects

A coarse grid can merge two nearby clusters; a fine grid can fragment one. Inspect multiple declared widths while keeping the color domain comparable. Points exactly on the extent edge need a documented inclusion rule. Export each bin's identifier, center or polygon, count, exposure and suppression state so the chart can be checked without its pixels. The export manifest should retain projection, extent, width and origin. An accessible summary should identify the highest-count cells and explain the unit encoded by color.

Worked contract

from collections import Counter
from math import floor, isfinite

def audit_spatial_counts(points: list[tuple[float, float]],
                         cell_width: float) -> Counter[tuple[int, int]]:
    if not isfinite(cell_width) or cell_width <= 0:
        raise ValueError("cell width must be positive")
    if any(not isfinite(x) or not isfinite(y) for x, y in points):
        raise ValueError("coordinates must be finite")
    return Counter((floor(x / cell_width), floor(y / cell_width))
                   for x, y in points)

depot_coordinates = [(47.2, 81.6), (47.7, 81.1), (59.4, 81.5)]
audit = audit_spatial_counts(depot_coordinates, 4)
assert audit[(11, 20)] == 2 and sum(audit.values()) == 3

Performance and operating cost

This rectangular audit grid takes O(N) expected time and O(B) space for N points and B occupied bins. It checks count conservation before passing projected coordinates to a hexbin renderer; rectangular cells and hexagons do not share identifiers. The renderer decides hexagon placement and edge rules. A real map also needs projection and exposure joins versioned with its bin table. Preserve input and retained counts to detect losses.

Common Mistakes

  • Calling raw incident counts a risk rate.
  • Using degree-based cells as if they had equal ground area.
  • Changing grid extent between periods and interpreting bin movement as behavior change.
  • Hiding suppressed or zero-exposure cells as ordinary zero counts.

Bin 810 projected service calls at two widths. Reconcile counts to input, attach journey exposure by cell and compare the busiest cell with the highest incident-rate cell.

title: Small multiples: compare groups with honest scales and facet order
summary: Repeat one chart grammar across groups, then choose shared or local axes according to the intended comparison.
body:
Repeat one chart grammar across groups, then choose shared or local axes according to the intended comparison.

A facet is a repeated measurement frame

Small multiples split the same visual grammar into panels, one per group. They reduce line crossings and legend lookup when a single plot has too many series. The gain depends on consistency: each panel should use the same measure, time window, mark type and aggregation rule. A panel for customer tickets and a panel for revenue do not become comparable simply because they share a grid. Declare the measure before arranging panels. Keep a visible label on each panel; color alone is insufficient.

Shared scales answer magnitude questions

If the reader needs to know which depot has the largest delay, a shared y-domain lets equal heights mean equal values. Local y-domains can make a low-volume depot's variation legible, but a steep line then no longer means a larger absolute change. If independent domains are necessary, print the local minimum and maximum in every panel and avoid a headline about cross-panel magnitude. Axis integrity applies to every facet. For percentages, a fixed zero-to-one domain is often an honest baseline; for residuals around zero, a symmetric domain may expose sign and spread better.

Keep the time window and missingness aligned

Shared x-axes help readers distinguish a simultaneous event from a panel-specific shift. A region with no observations on Wednesday should show a gap, not compress its calendar so Thursday occupies Wednesday's position. When groups enter the system at different times, an aligned calendar makes the unequal exposure visible. Time-series gap rules should be applied before faceting. If panels use different time windows by design, label them prominently and avoid visual comparison of positions.

Order panels for the task

Alphabetical order is stable but often unhelpful when inspecting performance. Sorting by a predeclared baseline or current value can put high-risk groups first; automatic resorting on every hover makes the layout hard to track. Record the sort key and freeze it for an analysis session. Do not omit small groups without stating a threshold and the number omitted. Small-sample uncertainty often explains why an apparently extreme panel should receive inspection rather than a confident ranking.

Budget the screen

Thirty tiny panels may be technically complete yet unreadable on a phone. Allow searching or paging through stable groups while keeping the same scale contract. A summary panel can show the total or reference band, but it must follow the same population rules. Test keyboard order and screen-reader panel labels. If each facet needs a unique tooltip, interaction cost grows with the number of panels; prioritize a simple data table for exact values. A chart grid should make comparisons easier, not force the reader to memorize dozens of legends.

Worked contract

from math import isfinite

def facet_domains(series: dict[str, list[float]],
                  shared: bool) -> dict[str, tuple[float, float]]:
    if not series or any(not values for values in series.values()):
        raise ValueError("each facet needs observed values")
    if any(not isfinite(value) for values in series.values() for value in values):
        raise ValueError("non-finite plotted value")
    if shared:
        values = [value for group in series.values() for value in group]
        domain = (min(values), max(values))
        return {name: domain for name in series}
    return {name: (min(values), max(values)) for name, values in series.items()}

depot_delays = {"north": [18, 47], "south": [3, 8]}
assert facet_domains(depot_delays, True)["south"] == (3, 47)
assert facet_domains(depot_delays, False)["south"] == (3, 8)

Performance and operating cost

For N values across G groups, scanning domains takes O(N + G) time. The shared branch stores an extra O(N) flattened list for clarity; a streaming minimum and maximum reduce that auxiliary memory to O(1), while the returned G domains still need O(G) space. Rendering cost scales with both the number of panels and marks. A UI that rerenders every facet after each filter may become slow even when the domain calculation is cheap; memoize by the complete filter and data-version key only when measurements justify it.

Common Mistakes

  • Using independent y-domains while claiming one group has the larger magnitude.
  • Dropping missing dates and shifting one panel's x positions relative to the rest.
  • Reordering facets during interaction without labeling the sort key.
  • Suppressing tiny cohorts without reporting how many groups were hidden.

title: Mosaic plots: make cell area match the underlying count
summary: Use widths and conditional heights to expose how two categorical variables share one total.
body:
Use widths and conditional heights to expose how two categorical variables share one total.

Choose a denominator before drawing tiles

A two-way mosaic plot partitions one rectangle by a contingency table. Each first-category column gets width proportional to its count in the full data set. Within that column, second-category tile heights represent conditional shares. Multiplying width by height yields the cell's share of the grand total. That area contract is the point of the chart. If the column widths are all equal instead, the display answers a different question: it emphasizes within-group composition and conceals unequal group sizes. Stacked bars are often easier to read when exact conditional rates are the primary comparison, while treemaps use area for hierarchical totals rather than a two-way cross-classification.

Declare the table grain

Count one unit only once in the table unless the chart explicitly represents events rather than entities. If a shipment can appear in several outcome categories, a standard contingency table is not valid until a mutually exclusive rule is chosen. A missing outcome is its own category or an explicit exclusion; quietly dropping it changes every tile's area. Aggregation grain and denominator should be fixed upstream. Record the category order even if one group has a zero count, and distinguish a true zero cell from a category never collected. Reconcile each column subtotal with source records before calculating widths, then reconcile all columns to the grand total. A plot that looks rectangular can still be numerically wrong.

Read association without mistaking size for rate

A wider group contributes more observations, while a taller tile within that group represents a larger conditional share. Readers often compare tile heights across groups and forget the width, or compare areas when the question is only about rates. Label both count and within-group percentage in a companion table. If a tiny tile cannot hold text, put the label outside or leave it to an accessible table rather than enlarging the tile. Heatmaps can encode a rate in color, but their equal-size cells do not show count automatically. Do not imply statistical significance from a striking mosaic pattern; sampling design, uncertainty and multiple subgroup inspections remain separate questions.

Keep order and coverage stable

A mosaic is more legible with a limited number of well-defined categories. Many thin columns or slivers make the visual fragile on phones and at high zoom. Sort categories by a declared business order, not by whichever tile creates the strongest pattern in each filter state. If a dashboard filter removes units, recompute column totals and display the new grand total; a stale denominator can make area and labels disagree. Linked filters should expose which cohort is selected. Export the exact cross-tabulation with count, row total, grand total, conditional percentage and excluded count so the visible geometry can be independently reconstructed.

Worked contract

def mosaic_tiles(table: dict[str, dict[str, int]],
                 outcomes: list[str]):
    if not table or not outcomes or len(outcomes) != len(set(outcomes)):
        raise ValueError("groups and ordered outcomes are required")
    if any(set(cells) != set(outcomes) for cells in table.values()):
        raise ValueError("every group needs every outcome, including zeros")
    if any(type(count) is not int or count < 0
           for cells in table.values() for count in cells.values()):
        raise ValueError("counts must be nonnegative integers")
    group_totals = {group: sum(cells.values()) for group, cells in table.items()}
    if any(total == 0 for total in group_totals.values()):
        raise ValueError("empty groups need a separate missing-data state")
    grand_total = sum(group_totals.values())
    tiles, left = [], 0.0
    for group, cells in table.items():
        right = left + group_totals[group] / grand_total
        bottom = 0.0
        for outcome in outcomes:
            top = bottom + cells[outcome] / group_totals[group]
            tiles.append((group, outcome, left, right, bottom, top,
                          cells[outcome]))
            bottom = top
        left = right
    return tiles

review_counts = {
    "early shift": {"accepted": 47, "returned": 13},
    "late shift": {"accepted": 20, "returned": 20},
}
review_tiles = mosaic_tiles(review_counts, ["accepted", "returned"])
early_accepted = review_tiles[0]
assert abs((early_accepted[3] - early_accepted[2]) *
           (early_accepted[5] - early_accepted[4]) - 0.47) < 1e-12
assert review_tiles[-1][-1] == 20

Performance and operating cost

For G groups and K outcome categories, validation and tile construction take O(GK) time and O(GK) output space. The positions are normalized to a unit square; the first tile covers 47 percent of the area because 47 of 100 reviewed shipments fall in that cell. Floating-point boundaries are drawing coordinates, not replacement counts. Keep the integer table available for labels and audit exports.

Common Mistakes

  • Making every group equally wide while claiming tile area represents total count.
  • Dropping unknown outcomes without updating the denominator and exclusion note.
  • Enlarging tiny tiles to fit labels, which breaks the area contract.
  • Reading an attractive pattern as evidence of association without examining uncertainty or sampling.

Validation drill

Cross-tabulate 83 inspected shipments by shift and disposition, including an unknown disposition. Reconcile the grand total and verify that each tile area equals its cell count divided by 83.

title: Stacked bars: separate composition from volume and preserve denominators
summary: Use absolute and normalized stacks for different questions, and retain every segment count.
body:
Use absolute and normalized stacks for different questions, and retain every segment count.

A stack has two possible questions

An absolute stacked bar shows a total and its parts in the same unit. A normalized bar forces every total to one and shows the mix instead. These are not interchangeable. If depot A closes 47 of 81 requests while depot B closes 470 of 810, both have the same closed share, but the latter carries ten times the workload. Place total and share in adjacent views when both matter. Define the denominator before calculating either bar. The title should say whether the horizontal extent means requests or a fraction of eligible requests.

Keep categories stable

Assign each status one color and one position across periods. If a status disappears, retain its zero-valued place in the data contract rather than shifting every later segment. The unanchored middle segments in a stack are difficult to compare precisely; when one category is the focus, use a grouped bar or a separate trend. Sort bars by a declared metric, such as eligible volume, and keep that order fixed across comparison panels. Facet ordering follows the same rule.

Handle absent and ineligible records

A missing status is not necessarily a measured zero. If the warehouse omits unresolved requests, a normalized stack can show an apparently perfect closure rate even as the unobserved group grows. Reconcile segment counts to the cohort total, expose an unknown state, and reserve a separate no-exposure state when the denominator is zero. A percentage bar for zero eligible requests has no defined composition. Missing-state display should use a label or pattern in addition to color.

Audit every filter

When a dashboard filters by region or week, recompute each segment count from the selected cohort and normalize only after filtering. Do not average prior percentages. Tooltips and exports should include segment count, denominator and percentage; rounded shares may sum to 99.9 or 100.1, which is a display effect rather than a data error. Linked selections must update totals and segments together. Test one-bar, zero-cohort and category-absent states before release.

Worked contract

def composition_by_depot(
    counts: dict[str, dict[str, int]], statuses: tuple[str, ...]
) -> dict[str, dict[str, tuple[int, float | None]]]:
    if len(set(statuses)) != len(statuses) or not statuses:
        raise ValueError("statuses must be unique and nonempty")
    result = {}
    for depot, segments in counts.items():
        if set(segments) - set(statuses) or any(value < 0 for value in segments.values()):
            raise ValueError("unknown status or negative count")
        total = sum(segments.values())
        result[depot] = {
            status: (segments.get(status, 0),
                     segments.get(status, 0) / total if total else None)
            for status in statuses
        }
    return result

mix = composition_by_depot(
    {"north": {"closed": 47, "pending": 34},
     "south": {"closed": 470, "pending": 340}},
    ("closed", "pending", "unknown"))
assert mix["north"]["closed"] == (47, 47 / 81)
assert mix["south"]["closed"] == (470, 470 / 810)
assert mix["north"]["unknown"] == (0, 0.0)

Performance and operating cost

For D depots, S declared statuses and M supplied segment values, validation and construction take O(M + DS) expected time and O(DS) output space. Reusing a prebuilt status set removes repeated set construction in a larger implementation. Rendering a normalized bar still needs the absolute counts for labels and audit. The example treats an absent segment as observed zero only under the stated complete-status contract; without that contract, an absent segment must be marked unknown.

Common Mistakes

  • Reading equal-width normalized bars as equal workloads.
  • Dropping unresolved statuses before calculating shares.
  • Changing stack order between weeks and implying a category moved.
  • Averaging percentages instead of adding segment counts first.

Validation drill

Prepare 13 weekly depot bars with different cohort sizes. Show absolute and normalized versions, then remove one status record from a source extract and verify reconciliation fails rather than silently improving a percentage.

title: Likert diverging stacks: keep the neutral split and response denominator honest
summary: Build survey-response bars around a declared midpoint while retaining item counts, nonresponse and the ordered response distribution.
body:
Build survey-response bars around a declared midpoint while retaining item counts, nonresponse and the ordered response distribution.

Plot an ordered response, not a signed measurement

A Likert item records an ordered category such as strongly disagree, disagree, neutral, agree or strongly agree. A diverging stacked bar puts the disagreement categories to the left of a center and agreement categories to the right. It makes direction and balance easy to scan across questions. Yet the categories are ordinal: the spacing between adjacent labels is not guaranteed to represent an equal psychological distance. Do not claim a change from one category to another has a precise numeric magnitude merely because the bar uses equal-width units. The chart should preserve the original five counts and their order; a single favorable-minus-unfavorable score can hide a polarized item with many respondents on both ends. Stacked-bar composition explains the part-to-whole encoding, while signed diverging bars serve a different data type.

Declare the center and the neutral convention

For a five-category item, one useful convention splits the neutral share evenly across the center: half extends left and half extends right. It makes negative and positive segment lengths symmetric around a visually centered neutral category. The neutral response itself remains one category and one count; splitting its drawing width must never double its reported count. Other layouts keep the full neutral block on one side or omit it from the diverging calculation. These choices change the visual origin, so use one convention across every compared item and name it in the legend. The contract below returns segment endpoints, not a plotting-library call, so a renderer can draw exact intervals and an accessible table can show unsplit counts. The center position is a presentation rule, not a statistic. Baseline integrity applies as much to opinion charts as to numeric axes.

Separate item response from invitation count

If 83 people receive a questionnaire and only 59 answer an item, a bar normalized to 100 percent of answers describes those 59 respondents. It does not imply 83 people expressed an opinion. Show response count and missing count beside each item, and choose whether the displayed percentages use answered responses or all invited people. A survey can have different eligible populations per item because of branching, so a single global denominator may be wrong. Missing, skipped, not applicable and explicit neutral are distinct states. The worked example accepts an eligible count per item and uses answered responses for the five segments while returning the missing total separately. If groups differ in response propensity, equal-looking bars can be misleading; inspect who answered before interpreting a difference. Grain and denominator and cohort filters make that comparison auditable.

Compare the distribution before sorting the questions

Sorting items by net agreement can help locate extremes but can also hide the questionnaire's intended order. Declare the sort key and preserve a stable question ID, especially if a dashboard allows resorting. For paired waves, compare like-for-like populations and wording; a changed label or response option can move a bar without a real attitude change. Small subgroups deserve visible sample counts and, where appropriate, an uncertainty display rather than a bold ranking. Use a consistent left-to-right palette whose labels are readable without color. The full five-category distribution belongs in the accompanying table, including neutral and missing counts. Avoid stacked bars so narrow that individual slices disappear; a small-multiple table or grouped display can be clearer for close comparisons. Small-sample display, shared scales and text alternatives support that choice.

Worked contract

RESPONSE_ORDER = ("strongly_disagree", "disagree", "neutral",
                  "agree", "strongly_agree")

def likert_layout(items: list[tuple[str, int, dict[str, int]]]):
    seen_items = set()
    output = []
    for item_id, eligible, counts in items:
        if (not item_id or item_id in seen_items or
                not isinstance(eligible, int) or eligible <= 0 or
                set(counts) != set(RESPONSE_ORDER) or
                any(not isinstance(counts[key], int) or counts[key] < 0
                    for key in RESPONSE_ORDER)):
            raise ValueError("items need unique IDs, eligibility and five counts")
        seen_items.add(item_id)
        answered = sum(counts.values())
        if answered == 0 or answered > eligible:
            raise ValueError("answered count must be positive and at most eligible")
        shares = {key: counts[key] / answered for key in RESPONSE_ORDER}
        neutral_half = shares["neutral"] / 2
        cursor = -(shares["strongly_disagree"] + shares["disagree"] + neutral_half)
        segments = []
        for key, width in (("strongly_disagree", shares["strongly_disagree"]),
                           ("disagree", shares["disagree"]),
                           ("neutral_left", neutral_half),
                           ("neutral_right", neutral_half),
                           ("agree", shares["agree"]),
                           ("strongly_agree", shares["strongly_agree"])):
            segments.append((key, cursor, cursor + width))
            cursor += width
        output.append({"item": item_id, "eligible": eligible,
                       "answered": answered, "missing": eligible - answered,
                       "counts": counts.copy(), "segments": segments})
    return output

survey = [("onboarding-clarity", 83,
           {"strongly_disagree": 5, "disagree": 7, "neutral": 11,
            "agree": 23, "strongly_agree": 13})]
layout = likert_layout(survey)[0]
assert (layout["answered"], layout["missing"]) == (59, 24)
assert abs(layout["segments"][0][1] + 17.5 / 59) < 1e-12
assert abs(layout["segments"][2][2]) < 1e-12
assert abs(layout["segments"][-1][2] - 41.5 / 59) < 1e-12
assert layout["counts"]["neutral"] == 11

Performance and operating cost

For I items and a fixed five-response scale, validating counts and constructing segment endpoints costs O(I) time and O(I) output space. With a configurable K-category scale, the same approach is O(IK) in time and space. The worked item has 59 answers among 83 eligible people, leaving 24 missing. Its 11 neutral answers are displayed as two widths of 5.5 divided by 59, but still reported as 11 respondents. The left edge is negative 17.5 divided by 59 and the right edge positive 41.5 divided by 59; those lengths sum to one answered-response unit. They are drawing coordinates, not a claim that attitudes are numeric distances.

Common Mistakes

  • Treating nonresponse as neutral or silently removing missing counts from the report.
  • Counting neutral twice after drawing half its width on each side of the center.
  • Mixing percent of answered respondents with percent of all eligible people across items.
  • Ranking tiny subgroups as if a few answers establish a stable preference order.

Validation drill

Collect 47 survey items with item-specific eligible counts. For each, reconcile all five answers and missing records, produce centered segments with the same neutral convention, and compare the chart with an accessible count table before sorting items by net agreement.

title: Chart exports: carry the data, filters and render contract together
summary: Give exported images an auditable data table and a compact manifest of the choices that produced them.
body:
Give exported images an auditable data table and a compact manifest of the choices that produced them.

An image is not the full evidence

A PNG captures pixels; it does not preserve the records, filter predicates, missingness states or exact values behind them. SVG retains scalable geometry, but it can still omit the underlying analytical contract. For a decision-grade chart, export an image, a machine-readable table of plotted values and a manifest describing the query and rendering choices. The package should answer which source snapshot, cohort, units, time zone, grouping rule, axis domain, palette and code version produced the picture. Dashboard provenance supplies these ingredients; export binds them to an artifact.

Version the plotted data product

A chart may use raw events, daily aggregates or a reduced display level. The export must name that level. Include a dataset snapshot or immutable revision, plus the report's as-of time when corrections are possible. A hash of canonical manifest bytes detects accidental changes to the manifest; it does not authenticate a source by itself. If integrity across systems matters, sign the package through a trusted release path. Never include private identifiers or unmasked rows merely because a chart view was authorized. Data classification still governs exports.

Keep visible and downloadable values aligned

The CSV or JSON table must use the same filters, denominator, sort, unit and missing-value policy as the displayed chart. If the chart shows rounded percentages, include underlying counts and unrounded rates in the data export while documenting the display rounding. A tooltip, table and image title should agree on the period and finalization status. Linked filters can change the cohort moments before a user clicks export; capture one state and one data version atomically for the whole package.

Make the visual portable and accessible

An SVG is useful for vector editing and high-resolution print, but font substitution and external styles can change its appearance. A PNG is more predictable but loses scale and selectable text. Include an accessible text summary and data table in either case. Document the output size, color profile where relevant, and the scale tick labels. Text alternatives should describe the main pattern, notable exceptions and uncertainty rather than repeat a generic chart title. For a public download, test that no hidden private series remain in SVG markup or embedded metadata.

Recreate before release

Re-run the export from its manifest in a clean environment. Compare plotted counts, axis limits, filters, title, source generation and checksum, allowing only declared rendering differences such as font rasterization. A changed query definition should make an old package non-reproducible by design; report that conflict instead of silently rendering with today's code. Keep an editorial preview for review, then publish an immutable artifact reference when the chart is used in a report or audit. Reduced series need the level and bucket rule in the manifest.

Worked contract

import hashlib
import json

def chart_manifest(query_id: str, dataset_version: str,
                   filters: dict[str, list[str]],
                   axis_domain: tuple[float, float],
                   plotted_rows: int) -> tuple[dict, str]:
    if not query_id or not dataset_version or plotted_rows < 0:
        raise ValueError("missing chart identity")
    if axis_domain[0] >= axis_domain[1]:
        raise ValueError("invalid axis domain")
    manifest = {
        "query_id": query_id,
        "dataset_version": dataset_version,
        "filters": {key: sorted(set(values))
                    for key, values in sorted(filters.items())},
        "y_axis_domain": list(axis_domain),
        "plotted_rows": plotted_rows,
        "unit": "minutes",
        "render_contract": "depot-delay-v3",
    }
    payload = json.dumps(manifest, sort_keys=True, separators=(",", ":"),
                         ensure_ascii=False).encode("utf-8")
    return manifest, hashlib.sha256(payload).hexdigest()

first = chart_manifest("depot-delay-week", "snapshot-81",
                       {"region": ["north", "north"]}, (0, 47), 31)
second = chart_manifest("depot-delay-week", "snapshot-81",
                        {"region": ["north"]}, (0, 47), 31)
assert first == second and len(first[1]) == 64

Performance and operating cost

For F total filter values and M serialized manifest bytes, sorting normalized filters costs O(F log F) in the worst case; JSON encoding and SHA-256 hashing take O(M) time and O(M) temporary memory. Exporting an image or plotted data can cost much more and depends on the renderer and row count. This hash identifies equal manifest bytes, not equal pixels or trustworthy provenance. Add a data-file checksum and a signed release record when the export package crosses a trust boundary.

Common Mistakes

  • Publishing only a screenshot when reviewers need the plotted data and cohort definition.
  • Exporting a CSV from a stale filter state while the chart shows a newer selection.
  • Assuming a manifest hash proves who created the data.
  • Embedding hidden private rows in an otherwise public SVG or HTML export.

Validation drill

Export one filtered depot-delay chart as SVG and CSV with a manifest. Change only the filter and verify the manifest digest changes, then rebuild the original chart from its saved version and compare counts and axis bounds.

title: Treemaps: validate hierarchy and leaf totals before assigning area
summary: Prevent duplicated parent values, unstable tiles and tiny unreadable leaves.
body:
Prevent duplicated parent values, unstable tiles and tiny unreadable leaves.

Area is a sum contract

A treemap divides a rectangle into nested areas proportional to a nonnegative measure. To compare storage used by product teams, assign each leaf one value and derive parent totals from those leaves. If a parent row already contains the total, summing it with its children doubles the area. Validate that every leaf has one parent, that the hierarchy has no cycle, and that the root total agrees with the source. Grain checks protect the basic unit before layout begins.

Labels cannot rescue tiny tiles

A rectangle's area is hard to estimate precisely, and small leaves cannot hold readable text. Use the treemap for broad composition and a sorted table or bar view for exact comparison. Group genuinely small categories into a named remainder only when their combined value and membership are reported. Do not simply omit leaves to make labels fit. Stacked bars often work better when the hierarchy has only one level or exact cross-category comparison matters.

Keep identity across versions

Many tiling algorithms can rearrange rectangles after a small value change. A user comparing two snapshots may see tiles move and mistake movement for a new category. Use stable IDs, a declared sort and a layout method chosen for the comparison task. If two versions must be compared, consider a fixed hierarchy with an accompanying difference bar; do not imply that a tile's new screen position has meaning. Shared-scale panels help only when the same root total basis is explicit.

Separate structure from measure

Zero-value leaves may be valid members of the hierarchy but have no visible area. Missing measures are different: they should be counted and surfaced outside the tiled display. A negative measure cannot be represented as area without a different visual contract. Tooltips should show path, leaf value, parent total and share; keyboard users need an ordered text tree or table. Accessible text can retain the small leaves that the drawing cannot label.

Worked contract

def hierarchy_totals(
    parent_of: dict[str, str | None], leaf_values: dict[str, int]
) -> dict[str, int]:
    internal = {parent for parent in parent_of.values() if parent is not None}
    if set(leaf_values) != set(parent_of) - internal or any(value < 0 for value in leaf_values.values()):
        raise ValueError("invalid leaf value")
    if any(parent is not None and parent not in parent_of for parent in parent_of.values()):
        raise ValueError("unknown parent")
    for start in parent_of:
        seen = set()
        node = start
        while node is not None:
            if node in seen:
                raise ValueError("cycle in hierarchy")
            seen.add(node)
            node = parent_of[node]
    totals = {node: 0 for node in parent_of}
    for leaf, value in leaf_values.items():
        node = leaf
        while node is not None:
            totals[node] += value
            node = parent_of[node]
    return totals

tree = {"all": None, "support": "all", "mobile": "support",
        "web": "support", "payments": "all"}
totals = hierarchy_totals(tree, {"mobile": 47, "web": 81, "payments": 31})
assert totals["support"] == 128 and totals["all"] == 159

Performance and operating cost

For V nodes, L leaves and maximum depth H, cycle validation and ancestor accumulation take O((V + L)H) time and O(V + H) space for totals and one ancestor set. A deep or very large hierarchy should validate and sum in one postorder pass, O(V). Production layout adds sorting, tiling and label placement. Every terminal node needs a nonnegative measure for area encoding.

Common Mistakes

  • Adding stored parent totals to leaf values and doubling displayed area.
  • Treating zero-area leaves as nonexistent members.
  • Reading a tile move between snapshots as a change in business structure.
  • Dropping tiny categories without reporting the remainder.

Validation drill

Build a three-level storage hierarchy with 47 leaves. Insert one duplicate parent total, one missing measure and one cycle; reject each before rendering, then compare the resulting treemap with a sorted leaf table.

title: Sunburst charts: reconcile the leaf ledger before drawing rings
summary: Build a radial hierarchy from one counted leaf ledger, keep parent totals consistent, and make narrow outer sectors inspectable.
body:
Build a radial hierarchy from one counted leaf ledger, keep parent totals consistent, and make narrow outer sectors inspectable.

One record belongs to one leaf

A sunburst partitions a whole into nested categories. The center represents the root, the next ring divides it into top-level groups, and each outward ring divides its parent again. Start from records or an explicitly aggregated leaf ledger, with one complete path per counted item. The same support ticket cannot appear once under Email and again under Chat unless the measure is deliberately ticket-channel events rather than distinct tickets. State that grain next to the chart. A root total of 47 tickets means every first-ring wedge must add to 47, and each branch must equal the sum of its immediate children when the branches represent totals. A separate parent count entered from another report is a common double-counting route. The preparation code below derives parent totals from leaves. Treemaps share the accounting requirement; grain and denominator checks establish what the area means.

Treat absent categories as data, not empty geometry

An incomplete classification is still a counted record. Give it an explicit category such as Unassigned at the first stage where classification is absent, or stop its path at a documented terminal node. Do not distribute its count across known children to make the ring appear complete. If one branch stops at depth two while another reaches depth four, the outer rings describe different levels of detail; the caption must say so. This lesson uses three-level paths so every ticket has the same depth and comparison is direct. Repeated label text in different branches does not imply the same node: the full path is the identifier. For example, Resolved under Email and Resolved under Portal are two separate sectors. Preserve full-path IDs in hover text, exports, and keyboard focus targets. Missingness and export manifests cover the adjoining data contract.

Read angular share against the right parent

A sector's angle communicates its share of the root at its depth, while a child-to-parent percentage answers a different question. Show both numerator and denominator in a tooltip or adjacent table. In the worked ledger, the Support branch contains 33 of 47 tickets, so it spans roughly 253 degrees of the first ring. Within Support, Email accounts for 19 of 33, not 19 of 47. A viewer cannot recover those denominators reliably from a small arc alone. Freeze branch order for repeated reports; re-sorting by the latest count makes equal categories move around the circle between periods. Use a stable color mapping for the first ring, then related shades or labels for descendants. If every small leaf receives a different saturated color, color stops carrying a useful meaning. Stacked bars are often clearer when only two levels matter.

Provide a route out of crowded outer rings

The outer ring can contain dozens of thin sectors even when its parent occupies a generous angle. Do not turn a two-pixel arc into the only way to discover a category. Expose a searchable hierarchy table with full path, count, share of parent and share of root. Keyboard users should be able to enter a branch, inspect children and return to the same focus position. If categories are grouped into Other, define the threshold in counts or root share, retain the original leaves in the downloadable ledger, and never combine categories across different parents merely because their labels match. A sunburst is strongest for following hierarchy and relative composition, not for precise comparison between distant narrow sectors. For precise ranking, pair it with a bar view. Chart accessibility and waffle charts offer alternatives for small shares.

Worked contract

from collections import Counter

def prepare_ticket_sunburst(leaf_ledger):
    totals = Counter()
    if not leaf_ledger:
        raise ValueError("leaf ledger cannot be empty")
    for path, ticket_count in leaf_ledger:
        if (not isinstance(path, tuple) or len(path) != 3 or
                any(not isinstance(label, str) or not label.strip() for label in path) or
                isinstance(ticket_count, bool) or not isinstance(ticket_count, int) or
                ticket_count <= 0):
            raise ValueError("each leaf needs three labels and a positive count")
        for depth in range(4):
            totals[path[:depth]] += ticket_count
    for path, parent_count in totals.items():
        if len(path) == 3:
            continue
        child_sum = sum(count for child, count in totals.items()
                        if len(child) == len(path) + 1 and child[:-1] == path)
        assert parent_count == child_sum
    return totals

ticket_leaves = [
    (("Support", "Email", "Resolved"), 14),
    (("Support", "Email", "Escalated"), 5),
    (("Support", "Chat", "Resolved"), 11),
    (("Support", "Chat", "Escalated"), 3),
    (("Billing", "Portal", "Resolved"), 8),
    (("Billing", "Portal", "Escalated"), 4),
    (("Billing", "Phone", "Unassigned"), 2),
]
totals = prepare_ticket_sunburst(ticket_leaves)
assert totals[()] == 47
assert totals[("Support",)] == 33
assert totals[("Support", "Email")] == 19
assert round(totals[("Support",)] / totals[()] * 360) == 253

Performance and operating cost

Let R be the number of leaf-ledger rows, D the path depth and N the number of distinct hierarchy nodes. Accumulating prefixes takes O(RD) time and O(N) space. The audit loop shown compares each parent with all nodes, so its simple form costs O(N²) time; for a large hierarchy, keep a child-sum counter during the same prefix pass and reduce reconciliation to O(RD + N). The code prepares totals, not drawing coordinates. A renderer assigns a parent interval first, then partitions that interval among children using the derived totals and a fixed category order. It must not sum the root and branch totals again as if each were independent data.

Common Mistakes

  • Counting the same record under multiple leaves without changing the measure definition.
  • Supplying independent parent values that exceed or disagree with their children.
  • Merging identical leaf labels from different parents instead of using full-path IDs.
  • Interpreting a sector's root share as its share of its immediate parent.
  • Leaving narrow outer-ring categories inaccessible without a searchable table.

Validation drill

Build a three-stage classification for 47 customer tickets. Introduce an Unassigned path for records lacking a final outcome, reconcile every parent with its children, and report both parent share and root share for the smallest leaf before drawing any arcs.

title: Aggregation grain and denominator: make every plotted mark auditable
summary: A visual aggregate is trustworthy only when each source row, grouping key and denominator have a declared meaning.
body:
A visual aggregate is trustworthy only when each source row, grouping key and denominator have a declared meaning.

Fix the source grain

A receipt table can contain one row per receipt while a status log contains several rows per receipt. Joining them and counting rows creates a review volume that rises when the workflow emits more events. Reduce the log to one terminal outcome per receipt before joining, or build an explicit event-level chart. Join cardinality is a precondition for visual accuracy.

Choose the denominator

A chart titled “review completion rate” needs a rule for receipts that were submitted but not yet eligible, rejected at intake or still open. Keep numerator and denominator alongside the plotted rate in the data contract. When filtering by channel, recompute both counts for the filtered cohort; never filter precomputed overall rates and average them.

Control time bins

A daily chart needs one time zone, one interval convention and an explicit policy for late events. A receipt submitted at 23:58 and completed after midnight might belong to the submission-day cohort even though its completion event occurs next day. Calendar policy keeps those two clocks apart. Document whether incomplete days are omitted or shown as provisional.

Reconcile the visual

For two channels with 34 of 47 and 18 of 23 timely receipts, the combined rate is 52 of 70, about 74.3 percent. The simple average of the two channel percentages is different. Test that the dashboard total uses summed counts. Include an empty group and one duplicated receipt ID to catch silent inflation.

Implementation

def weighted_completion_rate(channel_counts):
    timely = 0
    eligible = 0
    for timely_count, eligible_count in channel_counts:
        if not 0 <= timely_count <= eligible_count:
            raise ValueError("invalid channel counts")
        timely += timely_count
        eligible += eligible_count
    return None if eligible == 0 else timely / eligible

Performance and operating cost

Aggregating N rows by C keys is O(N) expected time and O(C) state with a hash map. Sorting labels adds O(C log C). A database group-by can move the work closer to the source, but its join and filter contracts still need inspection.

Common Mistakes

  • Do not average percentages when group sizes differ.
  • Do not count event rows as independent receipts.
  • Do not combine submission and completion timestamps without a cohort rule.
